## One problem you can understand by hand

**LeetCode 435 — Non-overlapping Intervals.** Choose the maximum number of non-overlapping meetings. A locally plausible rule such as selecting the earliest STARTING meeting can block many shorter ones.

A good algorithm explanation begins with the decision you need to make, not the method's name. Write down the smallest example and the exact choice available at each step.

## The approach that looks convincing but fails

Consider every subset of meetings and test overlaps. This is correct but expensive; choosing the wrong local rule is faster but wrong.

Do not improve the code yet. Ask whether the information you need is already present in a smaller version of the same problem.

## The key reasoning step

Sort meetings by FINISH time. Take the first compatible meeting that finishes earliest. It leaves at least as much remaining time for future meetings as any other choice.

## From actual numbers to mathematics

$$
a^*=\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{compatible}}}end(a)
$$

**What every symbol means:** A_compatible is the set of meetings that start after or at the previously chosen end; end(a) is the finish time of meeting a; a* is the compatible meeting with minimum finish time.

**Now substitute numbers into that same relationship:** Meetings A=[1,4], B=[2,3], C=[3,5]. Choosing earliest start A blocks B and C, giving 1 meeting. Choosing earliest FINISH B (end 3) allows C (start 3), giving 2. This small case exposes the important rule.

If a recurrence contains two alternatives, identify which real-world decision each alternative represents. If the formula uses a maximum, say what is being maximised and why the alternatives cover all legal choices.

## Why the result is actually correct

Exchange argument: take an optimal schedule and replace its first activity with the activity that finishes earliest. The replacement does not finish later, so it leaves all later chosen activities feasible and does not reduce the schedule's size. Repeat on the remaining interval.

A complete proof needs an initial state/base case, preservation of the hypothesis and an explanation that no valid possibility has been missed.

## Actual implementation

The [original, tested JavaScript implementation](../examples/patterns.mjs) exports `maxNonOverlapping`:

~~~js
import { maxNonOverlapping } from '../examples/patterns.mjs';

console.log(maxNonOverlapping([[1,4],[2,3],[3,5]]));
~~~

Run this from a `.mjs` file inside this topic directory. The same function is exercised by [the unit tests](../examples/patterns.test.mjs). The implementation is intentionally tiny so the recurrence remains visible.

## Study the complete implementation, one line at a time

Unlike a call-only snippet, this is the **actual small algorithm** used by the tested lab. Read the comments and match each state update to the worked numbers above.

~~~js
export function maxNonOverlapping(intervals) {
  const a = [...intervals].sort((x, y) => x[1] - y[1]);
  let end = -Infinity, count = 0;
  for (const [start, stop] of a)
    if (start >= end) { count++; end = stop; }
  return count;
}
~~~

**Walk through the important lines:**

1. Sort intervals by finish time; this order encodes the greedy-choice proof.
2. `end` is the finish of the most recently selected interval.
3. A new activity is compatible if `start >= end` (half-open meetings may touch at endpoints).
4. Keeping the earliest-finishing compatible meeting leaves maximum space for all later activities.
5. From `[1,4], [2,3], [3,5]`, select the second and third, for a result of **2**.

Run the [automated tests](../examples/patterns.test.mjs) after changing a condition to observe what fails.

## Complexity and failure conditions

**Cost model:** O(n log n) sorting followed by O(n) scanning, where n is meeting count; additional space depends on sorting implementation.

**A classic mistake:** Greedy is not 'always choose the biggest/best-looking thing'. The choice needs a proof. Coin values [1,3,4] and amount 6 defeat largest-coin greedy (4+1+1=3 coins, while 3+3=2); dynamic programming is required in the general coin-change problem.

In interviews, identifying **why a tempting shortcut fails** is more valuable than memorising one template. For example, a greedy choice needs an exchange proof; if no such proof exists, dynamic programming may be necessary.

Use only the numbers in the worked example and explain the state, choices, update, stopping condition, and why no better answer is excluded. Then change one assumption and explain what changes.
